## The question

[This graph isn't planar but doesn't satisfy Wagner's Theorem assumption?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5127324/this-graph-isnt-planar-but-doesnt-satisfy-wagners-theorem-assumption), asked by [jacek](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1634155/jacek) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2026-03-04; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> How is this graph not planar?  
>
> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
> Description so that post is clear without picture: $5$ vertices, let's say $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, with edges 
> $$\begin{align}
> A&: B, C, D, E \\ B&: C, D, E\\ C&: D, E\\ D&: E
> \end{align}$$
> ($X:A,B,C$ means edges $X$-$A$, $X$-$B$, $X$-$C$.)
>
> I am pretty sure that it is not planar (spent definitely too much time moving vertices around), but cannot find a $K_{3,3}$ or $K_5$ subgraph for [Wagner's theorem][q-2].
>
> What gives?
>
>
>   [q-1]: Ol0Xc0i1.png
>   [q-2]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagner%27s_theorem
:::

It's pretty clear from your description of $G$ in terms of vertices and edges that $G \cong K_5$. Each of the five vertices is adjacent to the other four.

You mentioned sliding around vertices, and I wanted to make sure you knew about [Graphviz][2]. It's a handy tool for laying out graphs. If you use the `circo` algorithm you can see the most familiar drawing of $K_5$.

[![Graphviz drawing of K_5][1]][1]
